title: Security Assessment and Testing
description: Making sure security controls are defined, tested and operating effectively: testing levels and techniques, testers and auditors, SOC reports and metrics.

nodes.title: Validation
nodes.description:
Gather the business requirements to understand what the business truly needs, and validate them with the relevant stakeholders.
Asks: are we building the right product?
You cannot do any of the testing in this map until you understand what the business needs.
Security should be involved in testing right from the start and throughout the system life cycle: gathering and validating requirements, defining controls, developing applications and systems, ongoing operation, and retirement and disposal of systems and data.
Exam hint: if asked when security should become involved in testing, pick the earliest possible answer.

nodes.title: Verification
nodes.description:
All the testing done once you start building the product.
Verifies that controls are properly designed and built into the system.
Asks: are we building the product right?

nodes.title: Rigour
nodes.description:
How much effort to invest in testing, from very little to a lot.
The value of the system to the organization drives it. The more valuable the system, the more testing you do, to be confident it supports the business in reaching its goals and objectives.

nodes.title: Testing a System
nodes.description:
Software is complex and often built by teams, so development is split into units.
Testing moves from single units, to the interfaces between them, to groups of units, to the whole system.

children.title: Unit
children.description:
Test each unit of software on its own, as it is developed.
Example (very simplified): an operating system has separate units for keyboard input, mouse input and video output. Each unit is tested separately.

children.title: Interface
children.description:
Units communicate with each other through standardized interfaces.
Interface testing verifies that communication between two or more units works correctly.

children.title: Integration
children.description: Once a few units are complete, test groups of units together to make sure they work well with each other.

children.title: System
children.description: Once all units are complete and integration testing is done, test the whole system.

nodes.title: Testing Techniques
nodes.description:
Techniques for performing tests.
They are not mutually exclusive: mix and match them to perform different types of tests.

children.title: Methods & Tools
children.description: The two main methods to perform testing.

children.title: Manual
children.description: Hands on keyboard: a person manually reads code, or performs actions on a running program.

children.title: Automated
children.description:
Automated tools: software that tests other software.
Examples: code scanning tools, vulnerability scanners.

children.title: Runtime
children.description: Whether the code is running or not during the test.

children.title: Static
children.description: Testing a system that is not running, by looking at the code.

children.title: Dynamic
children.description: Testing a system while the software is running.

children.title: Fuzz
children.description:
A form of dynamic testing.
Programmers are logical people: they expect logical input and produce logical output. Throw chaos at the system, massive amounts of random data, to find unexpected errors and vulnerabilities in the code.
Know the two types of fuzzers.

children.title: Mutation
children.description:
Often called dumb fuzzers.
They have no understanding of the input data or its structure. They randomly mutate existing input data to a system.

children.title: Generation
children.description:
Often called intelligent fuzzers.
They have a basic understanding of the type and structure of input the system expects, so they can generate new chaotic input.

children.title: Access to Code
children.description: Whether the tester has access to the source code, or only to the running system.

children.title: White
children.description: White-box: you have access to the source code for your testing.

children.title: Black
children.description: Black-box: you cannot see the source code. You test the running application, and its internal workings are a black box to you.

children.title: Techniques
children.description: A few of the key software testing techniques.

children.title: Positive
children.description:
Verify that the system works as expected.
Example: a correct username and password lets you log in.

children.title: Negative
children.description:
Test normal, expected errors.
Example: an incorrect username or password is handled gracefully. The system asks whether you forgot your password, and does not crash.

children.title: Misuse
children.description:
Abuse the system the way an attacker might.
Examples: testing for buffer overflows and SQL injection vulnerabilities.

children.title: Decision table analysis
children.description:
Tests system behavior for different input combinations.
Build a table of every input combination and its expected behavior, so you check all combinations and miss nothing, even in a complex application.
Particularly useful for complex software and requirements management.

children.title: State-based analysis
children.description:
Tests software that can exist in different abstract states.
Particularly useful for GUIs and communication protocols such as TCP.

children.title: Efficiency
children.description:
Techniques that reduce the number of tests needed while still giving the required level of confidence.
Example: a password must be 8 to 16 characters long. There is a boundary between 7 characters (rejected) and 8 (accepted), and another between 16 and 17. The boundaries create three partitions: 7 or fewer, 8 to 16, and 17 or more.

children.title: Boundary Value Analysis
children.description:
Find where the behavior changes (a boundary), then focus testing on either side of each boundary.
Formal definition: test cases cover the extreme ends of the input values.
Password example: test 7 and 8 characters, and 16 and 17 characters.

children.title: Equivalence Partitioning
children.description:
Divide (partition) the inputs into groups that behave the same way, then write test cases to cover each partition.
Password example: identify the three partitions and test within each one.

children.title: Operational
children.description: Testing systems that are deployed and in production.

children.title: Real User Monitoring
children.description:
RUM: monitor how real users use the system.
Tracks user transactions in real time for usage, performance and errors.

children.title: Synthetic Performance Monitoring
children.description:
Run scripted transactions to monitor functionality, availability and response times.
Small bots or agents simulate use of the system.
A good way to do load or stress testing.

children.title: Regression Testing
children.description: Done after a change to a system, to verify that previously tested software still works correctly.

children.title: Internal
children.description: A company's own employees test the company's own software.

children.title: External
children.description:
A company hires an independent external tester to test its software.
Can also mean a company sends its own employees to test a service provider or vendor, and the services it provides.

children.title: Third-Party
children.description:
Three parties are involved: the customer, the service provider, and an independent third-party auditor.
Third-party audits often produce SOC (Service Organization Controls) reports.
As security professionals, we want SOC 2 Type 2 reports.

children.title: SOC 1
children.description:
Focuses on financial reporting risks.
Not very interesting to security professionals.
Like SOC 2, comes as a Type 1 or Type 2 report.

children.title: SOC 2
children.description:
Focuses on the 5 trust principles:
- Security
- Availability
- Confidentiality
- Processing Integrity
- Privacy
Definitely of interest to security professionals.
SOC 1 and SOC 2 reports both come in two types: Type 1 and Type 2.

children.title: Type 1
children.description:
Applies to SOC 1 and SOC 2 reports.
Looks at the design of a control at a point in time. Essentially reviewing some paperwork on a Monday.

children.title: Type 2
children.description:
Applies to SOC 1 and SOC 2 reports.
Looks at the design and operating effectiveness of a control over a period of time, typically a year.
The auditors test, through sampling and other methods, whether the control operated effectively over the whole period.
Far more useful than Type 1.

children.title: SOC 3
children.description:
A summarized and sanitized version of a SOC 2 report, for public distribution.
Basically a marketing tool.

children.title: Roles
children.description: The roles that may be involved in the audit and assurance function.

children.title: Executive Management
children.description: Set the tone from the top, and promote and fund the audit process.

children.title: Audit Committee
children.description: Members of the board and senior stakeholders who oversee the audit program.

children.title: Security Officer
children.description: Advises on the security-related risks to evaluate in the audit program.

children.title: Compliance Manager
children.description: Manages the compliance program, so the company complies with applicable laws and regulations, professional standards and company policy.

children.title: Internal Auditors
children.description: Company employees who provide assurance that corporate controls are operating effectively.

children.title: External Auditors
children.description: Provide unbiased, independent assurance, because they are independent of the entity being audited.

nodes.title: Metrics
nodes.description: Define metrics as part of security assessment and testing, to measure what matters.

children.title: Focus
children.description:
Tie metrics back to business goals and objectives.
If you understand what the business is trying to achieve, you can create metrics that show whether it is making progress.

children.title: KPIs
children.description:
Key Performance Indicators: backward-looking metrics.
They show whether performance targets were achieved.

children.title: KRIs
children.description:
Key Risk Indicators: forward-looking metrics.
They show the level of exposure to operational risk, and help monitor potential future shifts in risk conditions or new emerging risks.
